candidates.title: Trust Calibration in Older Adults’ Human–Robot Interaction: A Dual-Path Model of Cognitive and Emotional Trust
candidates.abstract: As service robots are increasingly deployed in eldercare settings, trust calibration following robot errors has become a core issue affecting the effectiveness of human-robot collaboration. Focusing on older adult users, this study systematically investigates the joint influence mechanism of error situations and explanation strategies on trust calibration through a 2 (error severity: high vs. low) × 2 (transparency: high vs. low) mixed-design experiment, and further tests a cognitive–emotional dual-path model of trust calibration. Using video-based scenario simulation combined with scale-based measurement, the study was conducted with 80 older adults. Results show that high-severity errors significantly undermine both cognitive trust and emotional trust, with a more pronounced detrimental effect on cognitive trust. Transparency interventions primarily facilitate trust repair through the emotional trust pathway, with no significant direct effect on cognitive trust. The study further reveals that transparency is more effective in repairing trust under low-severity error conditions, and that individuals' technology anxiety significantly attenuates the repair efficacy of transparency on the cognitive pathway. These findings not only provide preliminary empirical evidence for a dual-path dissociation pattern in older adults' trust repair—characterized by emotional priority and cognitive lag—but also offer an important empirical basis and design directions for developing age-appropriate service robots with context-awareness, emotional interaction, and personalized adaptation capabilities.

candidates.title: Belief-based Risk-Aware Anticipatory Navigation: Modeling Intention and Position Uncertainty for Safe and Efficient Robot Navigation
candidates.abstract: The increasing deployment of Automated Mobile Vehicles (AMVs) in warehouses requires efficient navigation in dynamic environments shared with human workers. Traditional safety strategies, such as stopping or slowing down, often reduce efficiency and do not account for human-robot interaction. To address this, interaction-aware methods have been developed. However, traditional interaction models assume fixed parameters, rely on a single forecast, or use intent labels that are not updated during the interaction, and thus do not explicitly represent intention uncertainty, that is, variability in how people react to robots. When combined with position uncertainty introduced by sensing noise, this unmodeled intention uncertainty can make motion prediction and navigation decisions unreliable, leading to conservative behavior, inefficiency, or collisions in human–robot interactions. To bridge this gap, we propose Belief-based Risk-Aware Anticipatory Navigation (BRAN), a framework that jointly models intention and position uncertainty. BRAN maintains probabilistic beliefs over an agent's position and intention to explicitly represent uncertainty in both quantities. Position uncertainty is represented via sampled observations, and the intent belief is updated online through Bayesian inference so that predictions evolve with the interaction. These beliefs are propagated through the Social Force Model (SFM) to generate predictions of possible agent motion under uncertainty. We then compute collision risk from the predicted motion distribution and incorporate it into model predictive control as a constraint. This constrains predicted collision risk while optimizing motion toward the goal. Experimental results validate the proposed design in controlled settings, demonstrate its effectiveness in scenarios with multiple pedestrians, and confirm its feasibility on a real robot with onboard sensing and actuation.

candidates.title: Multimodal Socially Aware Framework for Human-Robot Interaction in Virtual Reality
candidates.abstract: Social robots must coordinate speech and movement while interpreting multimodal human input. We present a multimodal framework that integrates speech, vision, and touch to generate contextually appropriate robot speech and movement. We evaluated the framework in virtual reality with 18 participants across five social interaction scenarios, comparing its performance against a human-teleoperated baseline. Although participants rated the autonomous system above the neutral midpoint for both naturalness and social appropriateness, the teleoperated baseline received significantly higher ratings on both measures. Behavioral coding and qualitative feedback revealed that conversational timing, clarification of ambiguous requests, and spatial coordination were important factors contributing to this performance gap. These findings highlight key challenges in developing autonomous robots capable of natural, multimodal social interaction.

candidates.title: Gestures for Human-Robot Interaction
candidates.abstract: Human interaction involves the interplay of various communication media, including body movements, voice, gaze, and even written signs. In such an interplay, gestures and, more generally, body motions represent a fundamental communication channel. Due to the significance of gesture-based communication in human-human interaction, intelligent and embodied agents are expected to utilize its implications to interact with humans effectively. An embodied agent, like a robot, can reason and produce gestures as a bidirectional communication channel between itself and the human it is interacting with. To achieve full bidirectional, gesture-based communication, the same embodied agent should be able to both recognize and perform communicative and informative gestures. This chapter describes the different challenges characterizing gesture-based interaction models between humans and robots.

candidates.title: Design and Development of an AI-Based Voice-Controlled Robot for Intelligent Human-Robot Interaction
candidates.abstract: Most low-cost voice-controlled robots accept only a handful of fixed words such as “forward” and “stop”, and depend on a smartphone app for speech recognition. This paper presents the design and development of an AI-based voice-controlled mobile robot that holds natural spoken conversations and turns free-form requests into safe movements. The robot is built around an ESP32 microcontroller with an INMP441 I²S MEMS microphone, a MAX98357A I²S class-D amplifier and speaker, an L298N dual H-bridge driving two DC gear motors with wheels, a servo for head and gesture movements, and a 2S pack of 18650 lithium-ion cells with a main switch. A hybrid architecture is used: a compact keyword-spotting model on the ESP32 detects the wake word and a local “stop” command without any network, while the spoken request is streamed to an AI server where speech-to-text, a large language model and text-to-speech produce a structured JSON action and a spoken reply. A command validator on the ESP32 checks every action against a whitelist, speed limits and a time-out before the motors move, so the language model can never drive the robot outside its safe envelope. A review of 19 related studies shows that earlier robots offered either fixed-vocabulary control on cheap hardware or natural-language interaction on expensive platforms, but rarely both. Design calculations show that a 4-second request needs 128 kB of audio, well within the ESP32's memory, and that the battery pack supports an estimated 13.4 h of mixed use. An experimental protocol with metrics for recognition accuracy, latency, safety response and user experience is provided for prototype validation.

candidates.title: Trust me, I’m a robot: relational determinants of social robot acceptance among university students
candidates.abstract: Purpose Although social robots are increasingly being used in higher education‚ the relational antecedents of students’ acceptance of these robots remain unexplored. This study re-conceptualises the technology acceptance model (TAM) for social robots by shifting the theoretical focus from utilitarian beliefs toward the relational quality of the human–robot interaction (HRI), positioning trust‚ satisfaction and rapport as main relational antecedents of students’ attitudes and behavioural intentions toward social robots. The study also examines the moderating effects of user motivation‚ empathy‚ risk aversion and technology readiness on the attitude–behavioural intention relationship. Design/methodology/approach Cluster sampling was used to define the sample‚ which comprised 900 university students from six public universities in Greece. Structural equation modelling (SEM) was conducted with AMOS 29 to test the proposed model. Findings Trust‚ satisfaction and rapport are strong positive predictors of student attitude toward social robots‚ which in turn positively influences students’ behavioural intention to use social robots. User motivation‚ empathy and technology readiness motivators (optimism and innovativeness) strengthen the relationship between attitude and behavioural intention towards social robots‚ while risk aversion and technology readiness inhibitors (discomfort and insecurity) attenuate this relationship. Research limitations/implications Despite the contributions achieved here‚ there are some limitations that deserve to be mentioned and suggest promising paths for future research. Because this research used a cross-sectional design‚ it does not allow for causality and the possibility to observe how attitudes and intentions towards social robots develop over time. Future studies with longitudinal designs are needed to test whether the identified antecedents for establishing a relationship with social robots (i.e. trust‚ satisfaction‚ rapport) can increase or decrease with repeated social robot interactions (Donnermann et al.‚ 2022). Practical implications Given the tight connection of trust‚ satisfaction and rapport with students’ perceptions‚ it is important that institutions also consider the quality of the HRI when deciding whether or not to use social robots as teaching assistants. This includes the robots’ ability to build trust through reliable behaviour‚ provide satisfaction through responsive interaction and achieve rapport through attentive‚ empathic and positive communication (Buhmann et al., 2026; Lemon and Dhanesh, 2026). Originality/value This study adds to the literature by being one of the first to conceptualise social robot acceptance as a relational phenomenon‚ positioning trust‚ satisfaction and rapport as core antecedents of attitude and behavioural intention‚ a theoretical move entirely absent from existing social robot acceptance and educational HRI research. Beyond the direct effects‚ this study introduces two theoretically grounded categories of individual-level moderators: psychological-relational moderators (motivation‚ empathy and risk aversion) and technology-related moderators (technology readiness)‚ which collectively provide a coherent and empirically novel account of the boundary conditions governing social robot acceptance among university students.

candidates.title: Preclinical evaluation of a safety-aware multimodal robotic pipeline for human–robot interaction in post-stroke rehabilitation
candidates.abstract: Introduction: Post-stroke rehabilitation increasingly requires technologies capable of supporting intensive, measurable, and adaptable interventions while preserving clinical supervision and patient safety. This study presents a lightweight, safety-aware, and modular multimodal robotic pipeline for embodied human-robot interaction in post-stroke rehabilitation, with a first target application in hemispatial inattention. Methods: The system was implemented on the TIAGo mobile manipulator within a ROS 2-based architecture and integrates therapist-mediated supervision, speech-based and graphical interaction, head-orientation monitoring, adaptive auditory recall, robot-mediated and screen-based task delivery, and structured performance logging. Dialogue management is based on a deterministic finite-state machine coupled with a rule-based Natural Language Understanding pipeline, enabling predictable interaction handling, explicit fallback behavior, and therapist escalation for safety-relevant events. A preliminary preclinical evaluation was conducted in 16 healthy participants, with a repeated acquisition after 1 month. The study assessed operational feasibility, multimodal interaction robustness, head-orientation monitoring stability, task execution, ASR-related interaction events, usability, acceptance, and 1-month reproducibility of workflow execution. Results: All participants completed both acquisitions without adverse events or safety-relevant events requiring interruption of the experimental workflow. End-effector recognition accuracy remained high, attention-recall events were infrequent, screen-based visual tasks were successfully administered and logged, and usability and acceptance outcomes were favorable, with low anxiety toward the robotic platform. Discussion: These findings support the feasibility of using a therapist-supervised robotic platform as an integrated tool for structured interaction, head-orientation monitoring, rehabilitation-oriented task delivery, and quantitative logging. The study presents a preclinical evaluation of system architecture, safety-aware interaction design, and workflow robustness. Future work is organized in two stages: a dedicated acceptance and robustness protocol in healthy controls to formally test interaction acceptance, speech-recognition robustness, and safety-relevant failure handling, followed by a true rehabilitation protocol in post-stroke patients with hemispatial inattention, including therapist-supervised exercise adaptation.

candidates.title: Participatory design in human-robot interaction research: a systematic review
candidates.abstract: Participatory Design (PD) approaches for robot design offer promising avenues for enhancing technological innovation and aligning Human–Robot Interaction (HRI) systems with user needs. Despite their potential, there is a lack of a comprehensive overview of how these approaches have been utilized within the field of HRI. This article presents a systematic review of the literature on how PD is applied in the design of HRI systems, highlighting its advantages and challenges. Data were collected by reviewing 102 selected articles published from 2008 to 2024 in leading scientific databases for robotics. We summarize and classify the selected PD studies based on stakeholder participation, methods, and outcomes, among other aspects. We also report on the contributions of PD methodologies to key HRI issues, including ethical challenges, robot autonomy, and human-robot conflicts. Findings show a growing number of HRI researchers using PD approaches, particularly in the context of social robots for healthcare and assistive services. However, we also found that a perspective where robots are considered the solution to every problem, without fully understanding the realities of the target community, is still prevalent and that some aspects of PD, such as equalizing power relations, situated-based action, and long-term stakeholder engagement, are often overlooked.

candidates.title: Heard Enough to Act: Early Tool Calling in Spoken Dialogue Systems
candidates.abstract: Latency-sensitive spoken agents must know not only which tool to call, but also when they have heard enough to act. Waiting for the turn to complete delays execution even when the request is already actionable. However, neither existing spoken agents nor spoken dialogue corpora define the earliest point at which a request becomes actionable. We introduce a synthetic spoken-dialogue pipeline that provides earliest-actionable-point supervision, marking when the observed speech grounds a tool and its required arguments. Through controlled task generation, speech synthesis and alignment, and gated annotation, we construct 26,694 dialogues totaling 786 hours across 48 domains, with disjoint training and test argument values. We additionally create an audio rendering of $τ^2$-bench for external evaluation. We train an omni-modal language model on this corpus, enabling causal, chunk-level decisions and partial-transcript generation for downstream call completion. The model achieves tool-state macro-F1 scores of 0.48 and 0.47 on held-out dialogues and the external benchmark, respectively. For correct calls, the estimated mean lead over a turn-end cascade, using the same formatter, is 1.8-2.0 seconds in-domain and 1.1 seconds on $τ^2$-bench. These results demonstrate a data-driven path toward spoken agents that act while listening. We will open-source the pipeline and the training scripts.

candidates.title: Advanced E-Collaboration and Human-Robot Interaction for Early Diabetes Detection in Healthcare
candidates.abstract: Early detection of diabetes mellitus is important to prevent serious chronic consequences such as cardiovascular disease, kidney failure, neuropathy. This study investigates a transformative screening system that overlays human-robot interaction onto an advanced e-collaboration system to diagnostic reach and accuracy. Humanoid robots are the major patient interface that collects biometric and lifestyle data using interactive dialogues. The use of humanoid robots is found to be highly feasible with over 86% patient satisfaction. The information gets integrated into a cloud-based e-collaboration environment for risk alerting through the use of intelligent multi-agent system and machine learning models like Extreme Learning Machines deep ensemble learning. Contemporary collaborative intelligent models with accuracy diagnostic of 90.57% - 99.6%. The convergence of interactive social robotics with networked e-collaboration enables a scalable real-time pervasive health care solution.

candidates.title: The Hidden Cost of a Friendly Face: Investigating the Effect of Agent Embodiment on Trust Loss in Conversational Recommender Systems After Misleading Health Claims
candidates.abstract: Conversational recommender systems (CRSs) are becoming pervasive technologies, supporting everyday decisions in domains ranging from e-commerce to health and dietary contexts. In these settings, there is a growing trend to deliver CRSs as embodied conversational agents (ECAs)–i.e. virtual agents with visible avatars, synthesised voices, and nonverbal behaviours that simulate face-to-face human interaction. Agent embodiment has been linked to greater engagement, perceived trustworthiness, and user reliance on agent recommendations. Yet, how embodiment shapes user responses when an agent’s recommendation is misleading remains underexplored. We argue this is an ethical blind spot with particular consequence in health contexts, where flawed recommendations may influence decisions with meaningful consequences for well-being. Drawing on literature from trust in human-AI interaction, recommender systems, and embodied conversational agents, we conducted a between-subjects experiment in a healthy recipe recommendation scenario to investigate how embodiment shapes trust loss along the dimensions of goodwill and qualification trust following a misleading health recommendation, and how any buffering cascades into users’ willingness to follow the recommendation and their intention to continue using the agent. The findings carry implications for the responsible design and deployment of embodied CRSs, particularly in health contexts.

candidates.title: VoxTurn: Answering Several Turn-Taking Questions in One Pass with One Model
candidates.abstract: A cascaded voice agent must decide, throughout each silence of its user, whether the user has finished their turn: answering too early cuts the user off, answering too late makes the agent slow. It often needs related decisions too: will the user soon go on, is speech during its own turn an interruption or a backchannel, is a sound speech at all. With open detectors, each extra decision costs another model or another call, and on the 14-language eot-bench they cut users off in more than a quarter of mid-turn pauses. Because they are trained on segmented utterances, this mismatch is the largest single source of error. We present VoxTurn, a 0.8B speech LLM that casts these decisions as multiple-choice questions, scores the hidden state of each option, and answers any set of them in one forward pass with a block-isolating attention mask, exactly as if asked one at a time. Trained on real conversational pauses with labels derived from their timing, and re-queried while a silence lasts, VoxTurn reaches 11.5% false cut-offs in English at a 300 ms latency budget, comparable to two commercial detectors, and a 14-language mean of 19.9%, the lowest among open models, at 8.3 ms per decision. In Pipecat and LiveKit it cuts off 17% and 9% of turns, and it ranks fifth of 24 in TurnBench end-of-turn detection without any TurnBench training data. The model, code and framework plugins are released.

candidates.title: MultiPartyTurnBench: Benchmarking Floor Control in Multi-Party Spoken Dialogue
candidates.abstract: Full-duplex speech systems must decide when to enter, hold, or relinquish the conversational floor, even as multiple speakers overlap or backchannel without taking it. Existing evaluations study dyadic turn-taking or end-to-end agent behavior, but lack a unified, controlled evaluation of genuine floor transitions against confusable non-events in multi-party settings. We introduce MultiPartyTurnBench (MPTB), a benchmark of 240 synthetically generated, channel-separated conversations spanning two to five speakers and six interaction types. MPTB evaluates two complementary tasks: End-of-Turn (EOT) detection distinguishes genuine turn completion from temporary holds, while Interruption (INT) detection distinguishes successful floor takeovers from non-floor-taking speech. Exact event-conditioned annotations enable causal evaluation using false-positive-constrained recall and signed latency. Across acoustic, semantic, and turn-projection baselines, we find a stark asymmetry: learned systems achieve 82.5-92.6% EOT recall at 4.3-11.8% false-positive rates, while INT detection suffers from missed takeovers or excessive false activations. This asymmetry extends to five full-duplex agents which achieve 86.1-95.8% balanced accuracy on turn entry, yet perform near chance (46.9-54.7%) on selective interruption handling. Gemini-3.8-Live yields to 97.7% of backchannels, whereas MiniCPM-o-4.5 yields to only 1.4% of genuine interruptions. These findings establish selective floor control as a distinct, unresolved challenge for reliable multi-party voice interaction.

candidates.title: Reference-Guided Turn-Taking Style Transfer for Full-Duplex Spoken Language Models
candidates.abstract: Full-duplex spoken language models decide at every frame whether to take the floor, defining a conversational personality -- yet each set of weights encodes exactly one, which human speakers bracket rather than share. Existing controls mostly act from outside; none identifies the quantity that sets how much the model speaks. We identify it: a single late-layer residual-stream direction, the initiative vector, extracted from the model's own conversations without training or annotation. The same direction reads the decision, anticipating onsets up to 800 ms ahead, and shifts it: scaled during generation, it moves speech ratio from 6-12% to 42-61% (no steering: 21-30%), consistently across conversations, weights, and corpora. A short reference recording suffices to transfer a speaker's turn-taking style to the model, and the transfer is reference-specific: swapping in another speaker's reference worsens the match in 93-98% of cases, whereas the best uniform dose is indistinguishable from no steering. Turn-taking style is not frozen into the weights but a direction that can be read, shifted, and calibrated per person. Audio examples are available at https://elpsykongloo.github.io/initiative-vector/.

candidates.title: The impact of encouraging utterances by a human partner and a conversational robot on older adults’ subjective well-being: a 6-week sustained interaction
candidates.abstract: Introduction: In human-human communication, encouragement has been closely associated with subjective well-being (SWB). However, the long-term effects of encouragement in human-robot interaction remain unclear, particularly in comparison with human-delivered encouragement and across different encouragement strategy types. SWB comprises both affective well-being (AWB) and cognitive well-being (CWB). This study investigated whether sustained verbal encouragement from a human partner and a conversational robot could enhance older adults' SWB. Methods: A two-phase design was adopted. First, a preliminary online survey with 55 older Japanese adults (aged 65-74) was conducted to select encouragement strategies for the main experiment, identifying offering specific actions (high-efficacy) and distraction (low-efficacy) as two encouragement strategies that differed significantly in participants' perceived effectiveness (p < 0.05). Based on this survey, 18 older Japanese adults (aged 62-90) were recruited for an exploratory 6-week longitudinal experiment. Participants interacted with either a human partner or a conversational robot once per week and were randomly assigned to one of four conditions: human partner or social robot (RoBoHoN) crossed with high- or low-perceived-efficacy encouragement strategy. SWB was assessed using questionnaires, while post-session open-ended responses, diary entries, and post-experiment interviews provided qualitative data on encouragement experience, perceived SWB changes, and participants' perceived sources of SWB change. Results: Results suggested that high-efficacy verbal encouragement may positively influence older adults' SWB, possibly with a stronger effect than low-efficacy encouragement, with a crossover-like pattern emerging: for AWB, the advantage of high-efficacy over low-efficacy encouragement tended to be more pronounced in the robot condition (Δ gap = 2.8) than the human condition (Δ gap = 0.5), whereas for CWB, it appeared to be more pronounced in the human condition (Δ gap = 2.0) than the robot condition (Δ gap = 0.2); these crossover trends should be interpreted with caution given the small sample size. Qualitative findings further suggested that the conversation itself may have contributed to participants' perceived emotional support in the Japanese cultural context. Discussion: These preliminary longitudinal findings suggest that social robots and human partners may both contribute to supporting older adults' SWB and may play complementary roles.

candidates.title: “It feels like hard work trying to talk to it”: Understanding How Older Adults with Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) Experience and Repair Interactional and Conversational Breakdowns with Voice Assistants (VAs)
candidates.abstract: Designing Conversational AI systems to support older adults with MCI necessitates robustness in handling complex and personalized interactions. In this study, we investigate how older adults with MCI experience, navigate and attempt to repair breakdowns while interacting with a voice-based AI system in their homes for medication management through the lens of interactional ”seams”. Through a 20-week in-home deployment with 7 participant dyads, we analyzed 844 interactions to identify interactional and conversational breakdowns and user repair strategies. Drawing on post-deployment interviews, we reflect on the nature of these breakdowns and older adults’ experiences of mitigating them. We further illustrate how older adults draw on their situated knowledge and environment to make sense of and recover from these disruptions, highlighting the cognitive effort required in doing so. Our findings emphasize the collaborative nature of interaction in human-AI contexts, and point to the need for voice assistants to better align with users’ expectations for memory, their routines and external resources in their environment. We conclude by discussing opportunities for voice assistants to integrate contextual knowledge from older adults’ sociotechnical environment and to facilitate more meaningful and user-centered interactions.

candidates.title: D2: High-Capability Full-Duplex Spoken Language Models from Half-Duplex Backbones
candidates.abstract: Full-duplex spoken language models (FD-SLMs) support simultaneous listening and speaking, but often lag behind half-duplex spoken language models (HD-SLMs) in general capabilities. We propose Dialogue-to-Duplex (D2), a framework that converts pretrained HD-SLMs into high-capability FD-SLMs at fine temporal granularity. D2 adapts the original audio encoder to streaming through decoder-free representation distillation and learns full-duplex interaction through supervised fine-tuning. We systematically study the effects of chunk size on full-duplex interaction, general capabilities, and inference computation. We apply D2 to two distinct HD-SLM architectures, Qwen3-Omni and LLaMA-Omni 2. At a 12.5Hz update rate, Qwen3-Omni-D2 achieves 99.2% turn-taking success with 521-ms latency, 99.5% interruption success, and a state-of-the-art VoiceBench score of 70.1.

candidates.title: Social Robotics and Human–Robot Communication
candidates.abstract: This chapter explores the ergonomic, cognitive, and psychological mechanisms underpinning human–robot communication, focusing on the role of social robots in shaping human perception, behaviour, and socio-emotional engagement. By analysing factors such as robot design, embodiment, and communication modalities, the chapter highlights how these elements influence user interaction and the perception of robots as social entities. It examines the integration of verbal and non-verbal communication modalities, addressing challenges in reciprocity and robots’ behavioural appropriateness. The discussion extends to the implications of adaptive technologies like large language models, emphasising the balance between responsiveness and confidentiality in human–robot interactions. Furthermore, the chapter underscores the potential of social robots in workplace and therapeutic settings to enhance efficiency, safety, and emotional well-being of human interactants. By addressing user expectations and ethical considerations, the chapter seeks to provide a comprehensive framework for advancing social robotics applications in fostering meaningful human–robot relationships.

candidates.title: Emotional Sycophancy as a Safety Risk in LLM-Powered Social Robots
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being integrated into social robots, enabling more fluent, adaptive, and emotionally responsive interactions. However, prior research shows that the same mechanisms that make these systems socially engaging also create safety vulnerabilities. In particular, LLMs can exhibit sycophantic behaviour, validating a user’s emotional state or stated intention even when a safer response would require caution, correction, or refusal. This paper investigates emotional sycophancy as a safety risk in LLM-powered social robots. We present an exploratory study comparing model responses to matched prompts written in emotional and neutral tones in two risk-sensitive scenarios: child safety and financial scams. We analyzed the results through thematic coding, semantic embeddings, a safety score based on similarity to safe and unsafe reference centers, and K-means clustering. The results indicate that emotional prompts were associated with lower safety scores, while neutral prompts elicited more cautious, risk-aware responses. Building on these findings, we propose a risk-aware architecture for LLM-powered social robots that introduces privacy filtering, emotional tone detection, risk classification, safety verification, response rewriting, and action governance before embodied execution.

candidates.title: Bridging design disciplines: a literature review of biologically-inspired design, human-centered design, and human-robot interaction
candidates.abstract: Abstract As robotic technologies become more integrated into society, there is a growing demand for systems that are not only technically robust, but also socially accepted, safe, and designed for long-term use. Biologically-Inspired Design (BID), Human-Centered Design (HCD), and Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) each offer valuable theories, methodologies, and tools to support the design and evaluation of such systems. Despite their complementary goals, these fields have largely developed in isolation. The lack of integration across BID, HCD, and HRI presents significant barriers for researchers and designers seeking to create biologically-informed, human-centered robots that facilitate meaningful interactions. In this work, an integrative literature review was conducted to examine the fields of BID, HCD, and HRI. An analytic categorization approach was used to categorize 63 papers into one or more of the three fields: 20 in BID, 27 in HCD, and 21 in HRI, with some papers categorized into multiple categories. Within each field, an inductive, interpretive coding and thematic analysis were used to identify key terminology, tools, methods, and conceptual frameworks, helping establish a shared vocabulary and summarize the state of the art. This was followed by a synthesis of limitations and field-specific gaps. Cross-field analysis revealed only four papers demonstrating overlap within the reviewed corpus: three showing implicit connections between HCD and HRI, and one showing implicit overlap between BID and HRI with indirect ties to HCD. This review lays the groundwork for more integrated design research by identifying opportunities for collaboration across BID, HCD, and HRI, highlighting the potential for more biologically-informed, user-centered, and socially responsive robotic systems.

candidates.title: TurnTurk-GPT: Text-Based Turn-Taking Prediction for Turkish
candidates.abstract: This paper presents TurnTurk-GPT, a text-based turn-taking predictor for Turkish obtained by fine-tuning a Turkish GPT-2 model with the TurnGPT objective on synthetic and real dialogue, and evaluates it on real Turkish conversation against rule baselines, a zero shot Turkish language model and a widely used multilingual end-of-turn detector. Evaluation uses word-level decision points on unpunctuated, lower-cased text approximating the output of streaming speech recognisers, recording-disjoint and speaker-disjoint folds, nested threshold selection and paired cluster bootstrap tests. TurnTurk-GPT outperforms the multilingual detector under both recording-disjoint and speaker-disjoint evaluation. Its gain over a zero-shot Turkish language model is largest for speakers seen in training, while on unseen speakers it matches this strong baseline. Removing the suffixes of the turn-final word reduces AP by up to 44%, against 2% for a sentence-internal word, locating the Turkish end-of-turn cue in verb-final morphology. Synthetic dialogue alone yields the weakest trained model, and when a speaker pauses the zero-shot and multilingual baselines remain close to chance. The model and the evaluation protocol are publicly released.

candidates.title: StretchBot: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Adaptive Guidance with Assistive Robots
candidates.abstract: Abstract Assistive robots have growing potential to support physical wellbeing in home and healthcare settings, for example, by guiding users through stretching or rehabilitation routines. However, existing systems remain largely scripted, which limits their ability to adapt to user state, environmental context, and interaction dynamics. In this work, we present StretchBot, a hybrid neuro-symbolic robotic coach for adaptive assistive guidance. The system combines multimodal perception with knowledge-graph-grounded large language model reasoning to support context-aware adjustments during short stretching sessions while maintaining a structured routine. To complement the system description, we report an exploratory pilot comparison between scripted and adaptive guidance with three participants. The pilot observations indicate that the adaptive condition was rated higher for perceived adaptability and contextual relevance, while scripted guidance remained competitive in smoothness and predictability. These observations suggest that structured actionable knowledge may help ground language-model-based adaptation in embodied assistive interaction, while highlighting the need for larger, longitudinal studies to evaluate robustness, generalizability, and long-term user experience.

candidates.title: Bridging Human–AI Interaction and Human–Robot Interaction: Shared Challenges, Converging Futures
candidates.abstract: This panel examines the growing convergence of human–AI interaction (HAI) and human–robot interaction (HRI) as intelligent systems become more autonomous, embodied, and embedded in everyday settings such as healthcare, education, homes, and workplaces. Although HAI and HRI have evolved as distinct fields, the panel argues that shared human factors concerns—such as trust, safety, autonomy, teamwork, situation awareness, evaluation, and responsible deployment—now require greater integration across both domains. Drawing on perspectives from leading researchers and doctoral students, the session explores how embodiment, motion, social cues, and system transparency shape human interaction with AI and robots. It also addresses methodological tensions, including laboratory versus field evaluation and short-term versus longitudinal study, while highlighting implications for ethics, training, and design. Overall, the panel aims to identify common challenges, foster cross-disciplinary collaboration, and outline a research roadmap for human-centered intelligent systems that improve performance, well-being, and quality of life across diverse contexts and sectors.

candidates.title: Human-robot teams: an Input-Mediator-Output-Input perspective on a new work paradigm
candidates.abstract: In Human Resource Management (HRM), team performance is a central concern. For HRM, the integration of emerging technologies such as robots represents a novel way to leverage team performance. As organizations begin to integrate robots into work teams, HRM practitioners face the challenge of managing human-robot collaboration, including the complex team dynamics that arise. Yet, systematic guidance for HRM on how to integrate robotic assistants into teams remains scarce. Addressing this gap, we provide real-world insights based on an online experiment and an eight-week longitudinal field study. Our findings are synthesized in an Input-Mediator-Output-Input (IMOI) model of human-robot teams. We show that robot acceptance is shaped by the robot’s human-likeness in appearance – preferring android robots over humanoid robots – and by the alignment between expected and experienced robot competence. Furthermore, human team members prefer robots that offer high assistance while exhibiting reactive (rather than proactive) behavior. Over time, human-robot teams show higher effectiveness than human-only teams, particularly in later project phases. These findings suggest that integrating robotic assistants into teams can enhance long-term team performance. We provide recommendations relevant for HRM on fostering robot acceptance and team effectiveness in human-robot teams, contributing to the growing field of human-robot collaboration in the workplace.

candidates.title: Intelligent Robots for Elderly Care: Categories, Application Scenarios, and Challenges
candidates.abstract: Aging populations have increased the demand for intelligent, personalized, and emotionally supportive elderly care services. Traditional care models often face limitations such as high labor costs, insufficient service continuity, and limited emotional support. Deep learning-driven elderly care robots provide a promising solution by integrating perception, decision-making, human-robot interaction, and adaptive service functions. This paper reviews the major categories of intelligent elderly care robots, including rehabilitation robots, nursing robots, and companion robots. It further discusses their application scenarios in home care, nursing homes, and community-based care. Existing studies show that deep learning, machine vision, multimodal sensing, and large language models can improve motion assistance, health monitoring, emotional interaction, and personalized companionship. However, several challenges remain, including technical reliability, data privacy, ethical risks, high deployment costs, and user acceptance among older adults. Future development should focus on lightweight models, multimodal fusion, privacy-preserving learning, and human-centered design. Intelligent elderly care robots should not replace human caregivers, but should support them in providing safer, more efficient, and more compassionate care.

candidates.title: HUMAN ROBOT COLLABORATION AND AI-ENABLED WAREHOUSE SAFETY MANAGEMENT FOR SUSTAINABLE LOGISTICS OPERATIONS IN SAUDI ARABIA
candidates.abstract: Robotic warehousing offers opportunities to reduce hazardous manual transport while introducing new risks at shared workstations, aisle intersections and digitally coordinated handovers. This critical integrative review evaluates how human-robot collaboration and artificial intelligence can support safer, more sustainable logistics operations, with Saudi Arabia as the proposed implementation context. Thirty DOI - indexed publications dated 2020 - 2025 were purposively examined across operational research, ergonomics, robotics, occupational safety and logistics management. Evidence was organised around exposure pathways, collaborative task allocation, predictive sensing, safety assurance, workforce acceptance and organisational governance. The synthesis shows that robotics may reduce walking and handling demands, but operational benefits cannot be equated with verified injury reduction. Adaptive speed control, transparent intention signalling, fatigue - aware scheduling and human - centred training appear promising when embedded within independently validated safeguards. Conversely, sensor uncertainty, deadline pressure, opaque algorithmic decisions and fragmented system ownership may transfer rather than remove risk.

candidates.title: Sub-Millisecond Reflexes for Continuous Physical Human-Robot Interaction
candidates.abstract: Continuous physical human-robot interaction requires robots to rapidly adapt their control behaviour without interrupting task execution. However, existing ROS 2 control architectures rely on stop-to-switch mechanisms that introduce substantial delays and interrupt execution. We present an open-source, sub-millisecond reflex engine based on an enhanced ROS 2-compatible multimode controller that enables deterministic switching between control modalities and integrates reflex behaviours for mitigating contact hazards and kinematic limit violations. Experiments on a Franka Robotics manipulator demonstrate switching delays below 0.1 ms, more than four orders of magnitude faster than conventional ros2_control, while maintaining continuous operation during safety-critical events. In a multi-stage manipulation task, the proposed framework reduced execution time by 3.5% and peak trajectory jerk by more than threefold. By eliminating runtime middleware overhead, controller transitions are implemented as lock-free pointer operations, enabling reflex-level responsiveness within an open-source robotics framework.

candidates.title: Human–Robot Interaction and Ergonomics
candidates.abstract: Robots in the workplace are becoming a familiar sight. Hence, they have become the focus of debates and research on workplace ergonomics. While this emerging technology holds great promise to improve environments, this can only be achieved through the intentional application of ergonomic principles. Physical, cognitive and organizational ergonomics must be considered when talking about human-robot interaction (HRI) in a work environment. This chapter presents fundamentals on both human-robot interaction and ergonomics. This includes key topics such as potential roles of humans in HRI, interaction design and interfaces. Furthermore, it presents key domains of HRI and the emerging perspectives in research and application. It underscores the importance of an interdisciplinary approach in assessing the impact of robotics on humans and emphasizes the need for a human-centered design philosophy when developing innovative robotic systems.

candidates.title: Fixed-Reference Pose Residuals for Measuring Cross-Dataset Cue Transfer in Human-Robot Interaction Anticipation
candidates.abstract: Social and service robots in public spaces need to anticipate which nearby person is about to approach and touch them, so that a response can be prepared before contact. It is largely unknown which cues support this anticipation when a model trained with one robot is used on another robot at a different site. We study this question with a fixed-reference pose residual (FRPR) model: a geometry predictor built from the person's bounding box and mask is trained and frozen, and a temporal network then learns from body pose an additive correction to its logit, so that every prediction splits exactly into a geometry term and a pose term. Between two public egocentric datasets recorded by different robots, HUI360 and SSUP-A, with every choice made on source data, the pose correction raised average precision (AP) from 0.277 to 0.321 from SSUP-A to HUI360 and gave no measurable gain in the opposite direction; the same asymmetry held over a stronger, source-selected geometry reference. Freezing gave no AP advantage over joint training, and simple geometric baselines and tree ensembles remained competitive or better, so the construction serves measurement rather than prediction accuracy. A head-orientation residual added small gains in both directions. Post hoc, whether a person faces the camera kept its discriminative direction across datasets, whereas head pitch reversed. With thresholds chosen on source data, the neural models that use geometry detected at most 17% of target interactions. Code and processed data are available at https://github.com/WeiZhou96/FRPR-interaction-anticipation.

candidates.title: Towards inclusive education mediated by social robotics: trainee educators' perceptions of robotic systems analysis
candidates.abstract: Among the transformations shaping contemporary educational contexts, social robotics is emerging as an innovative technological field capable of introducing physical presence, communication dynamics and multimodal forms of interaction (Neumann, 2023). Unlike other digital technologies, social robots not only perform functions related to instructional support, communication facilitation and adaptive learning (Woo et al., 2021; Youssef et al., 2023), but provided that the intended educational objectives are clearly defined they can also directly influence the emotional and relational dimensions of the educational experience (Martinez-Roig, 2024), affecting interaction patterns, student participation (Woo et al., 2021), motivation and support throughout learning activities (Youssef et al., 2023). In this regard, the use of social robots in educational settings does not automatically lead to improved student learning outcomes. Rather, their effectiveness depends closely on the quality of the learning experience they help create, the role assigned to robotics within educational activities and the extent to which educators and teachers understand and interpret both the opportunities and limitations of social robotics (Mullick, 2025). Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 56-59. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. Volume DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23211262. Section: Social Robotics and Socio-Emotional Inclusion.

candidates.title: TARSphere: A Robot-Oriented Full-Stack Framework for Long-Horizon Embodied Agents in Evolving Physical and Social Environments
candidates.abstract: Robots must act under physical and social constraints while adapting to changes in their environment and human needs. Existing embodied-agent systems often focus on specified goals or abstract execution into symbolic actions, limiting evaluation in an evolving world. We introduce TARSphere, a robot-oriented full-stack framework for physically and socially grounded long-horizon embodied agents. TARSphere-Infra runs robot policies in a physics simulator with embodied NPCs and constrained dialogue. An event-driven finite-state machine (FSM) uses completed actions and delivered information to update task states and evaluate outcomes. TARSphere-Harness, its embodied brain harness, lets a frozen multimodal large language model (MLLM) act through multi-level executable skills, using observations, hierarchical memory, and execution feedback to revise its decisions. On this foundation, agent-in-the-loop curation aligns task semantics, causal dependencies, and scene geometry to construct TARSphere-Bench: 360 episodes across 30 indoor scenes. Five paired conditions assess perceptual robustness, disruption adaptation, task update, human coordination, and intent understanding for navigate-and-report and fetch-and-deliver tasks. Our evaluation of 8 MLLMs shows that general-purpose models can outperform embodied models, while task updates and human interaction remain difficult. Frequent collisions and falls further motivate evaluating execution safety alongside task success, even with a shared action interface and decision budget.

candidates.title: HFE Considerations in Sustainability in Robotics
candidates.abstract: Sustainability can be conceptualized as three interlinked aspects: economic; social; and natural capital. In this chapter we will examine what is required for each of these aspects from a human factors and ergonomics perspective to enable sustainability in human-robotic systems. When looking at the economic and social capital nexus it is important to take into account issues of safety and the future roles of humans in robotic systems. This includes issues such as skills, training, resilience, and employment status of the humans. Furthermore, the possibilities arising from advanced social robotics also requires an examination of issues such as privacy, trust, and understandability. When looking at the economic and natural capital nexus it is necessary to consider aspects such as the materials used to produce, maintain, and deconstruct robotic systems as well as the eco-efficiencies and eco-effectiveness that can be obtained from including robotics in human systems. Such an examination requires a consideration of the diverse impact of robotic systems in different geographical communities, and among regions with different economic development status. The social and natural capital nexus requires us to evaluate when and where to invest in human-robotic systems, but also when and where to resist such developments. Finally, we consider the HFE values that are needed to help develop a more sustainable approach to the development of human-robotic systems.

candidates.title: LLM-Based Waypoint Authoring via Augmented Reality for Human–Robot Interaction
candidates.abstract: Augmented reality (AR) can make robot programming more intuitive by letting users set motion parameters directly in the workspace. This paper extends AURaPath, an AR system for interactive 6-DoF waypoint determination on a UR10 collaborative robot using HoloLens2, with a voice modality for hands-free authoring. The voice layer follows a two-tier design: an on-device keyword recognizer handles the safety-critical verbs behind a two-step confirmation gate, and a large language model (LLM) maps the resulting transcript to the system’s structured command set so that operators need not memorize fixed phrases; the deployed pipeline takes spoken microphone input, while the benchmark below evaluates the transcript-to-command mapping stage in isolation. We evaluate the mapping layer on an objective benchmark of 169 labeled utterances that isolates language-to-command mapping from speech recognition and robot execution, and we compare a deterministic keyword baseline, four local models on a single consumer GPU, and free-tier cloud backends. The keyword baseline cannot express parameterized authoring commands and scores zero on every authoring field, while a free-tier cloud model reaches 95.3% exact-match results, averaged over 10 runs. The reject analysis shows that the ability to decline out-of-scope input, rather than raw accuracy, determines whether a model is suitable for the language-mapping tier of our safety-gated architecture, in which a deterministic layer and a preview-before-execute gate remain responsible for execution, which supports keeping the safety-critical verbs on the deterministic layer. The benchmark selects the backend that the deployed system uses, on the same physical UR10 demonstrated in the base system. The project code, the evaluation harness and dataset, and the base-system demonstration are available on GitHub (Please see Data Availability Statement section).

candidates.title: “Cute Companion” or “Awful Thing”: Understanding Individual Differences in Attitudes to Social Robots as Pets
candidates.abstract: Abstract For users unable to keep pets due to logistical, financial, or health reasons, social robots could offer a substitute. However, these robots remain uncommon in domestic use, and it is unclear how individual user traits or robot attributes impact receptivity or perceptions toward social robots as pets. We conducted a mixed-methods survey exploration ( N = 163) of respondents’ initial receptivity and preconceptions regarding five robots with varied morphologies to understand whether these perceptions correlated with individual traits. We found that indi-vidual differences in anthropomorphism propensity, pet attachment and lower age all predicted positive initial perceptions of the social robots as domestic com-panions, guiding future expectations. Furthermore, a divide emerged between participants with non-negotiable philosophical objections to robot pets and those with addressable concerns around robot fidelity and agency. We discuss the impli-cations of user perceptions on the current feasibility of domestic robot pets and provide actionable directions for robot development.

candidates.title: Towards Multilingual End-of-Turn Detection using Frozen Speech Encoders
candidates.abstract: A spoken dialogue system must judge when the user has yielded the floor. This end-of-turn (EoT) detector is normally trained and tuned afresh for each language, which is costly to scale to new languages. We instead build one on a frozen multilingual encoder, training only a small fixed-size head. Using five CALLHOME languages, we investigate three questions. First, how well a head trained on one language transfers zero-shot to the others. Second, how much target-language adaptation is required to recover full task performance. Third, whether a single fixed decision threshold holds across languages without per-language tuning. We find that the head transfers well, even between tonal and pitch-accent languages, and that a few hours of audio recover nearly all the loss, matching in-language training. A frozen multilingual encoder with one lightweight head is a practical, language-agnostic baseline for EoT detection.

candidates.title: Challenges and design requirements for public-facing social robots
candidates.abstract: Public-facing social robots are increasingly being introduced into environments such as airports, libraries, hospitals, and campuses to provide information, assistance, and engagement. Their operation in these open and dynamic settings introduces complex challenges that cut across privacy, cybersecurity, ethics, usability, and regulation. While existing studies have explored these dimensions separately, few have examined how they intersect in real-world deployments. This study draws on semi-structured interviews with twenty-one multidisciplinary experts to identify cross-cutting risks and practical design requirements for public-facing social robots. Thematic analysis identified interrelated challenges concerning technical capabilities, public interaction, and organisational conditions, including risks associated with third-party components. Experts emphasized privacy- and security-by-design principles, adaptive and inclusive interaction, resilient technical architectures, and certification mechanisms for responsible deployment. The study’s contribution is a context-specific synthesis that organizes these established engineering and governance principles around the conditions of public-facing deployment. The resulting requirements and indicators are presented as candidate guidance for subsequent operationalization and validation, rather than as validated engineering standards.

candidates.title: "It Would Make a Geordie Feel at Home": Regional Accent Perceptions and Speech Accommodation in Voice AI
candidates.abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems often perform less accurately for speakers of regional dialects, but less is known about how users respond to these limitations and how regional voices produced by voice assistants (VAs) are evaluated through a sociolinguistic lens. This study investigates these issues among speakers of Newcastle English (Geordies), examining both linguistic accommodation to voice technologies and perceptions of regional versus mainstream-accented VA voices. Participants interacted with a simulated VA that spoke either Newcastle English or Standard Southern British English (SSBE). They subsequently completed semi-structured interviews about their experiences with the experimental VA and voice technologies, language use, accent attitudes, and place orientation. The findings reveal a two-way process of sociolinguistic bias. The Geordie VA was associated with familiarity, warmth, personality, and local belonging, but also with concerns about professionalism and authority, whereas the SSBE voice was perceived as more neutral, clear, and credible. Participants also reported adapting their speech when voice technologies failed to recognise them, most commonly by shifting to a more mainstream accent, enunciating more clearly, and speaking more slowly. These strategies are similar to accommodation in human-human interaction and reflect users' perceptions of what technologies can recognise, also known as perceived intelligibility pressures. Overall, the findings demonstrate that voice technologies can reproduce existing accent biases both by encouraging users to suppress regional features and by activating established social stereotypes through synthetic voices. The study positions sociolinguistics as a bridge between understanding human-AI interaction and designing inclusive technologies around users' own linguistic priorities.

candidates.title: The Evolution of Human– Robot Interaction
candidates.abstract: This chapter deals with the evolution of human–robot interaction from early industrial automation to intelligent and immersive systems. It studies the key transitions that include the rise of collaborative robots, social and service robots, and learning-enabled robotic systems. The chapter highlights how advances in sensing, communication, and artificial intelligence have reshaped interaction. It deals with moving from command-based control to adaptive and context-aware collaboration. The role of extended reality is discussed as an accelerating agent for immersive and embodied interaction. It provides better human involvement during interaction. By addressing the ethical and societal dimensions, the chapter deals with HRI for long-term human–robot symbiosis.

candidates.title: How unequal is unequal? Turn-taking simulation for benchmarking participation and opportunity inequality in small-group collaboration
candidates.abstract: Participation equity is essential for ensuring that students gain cognitive and social benefits from collaborative learning, yet there is a lack of quantitative benchmarks for interpreting participation and opportunity distributions in small-group collaboration. This study focuses on two turn-based analytical dimensions of participation equity: participation equality, measured by students' shares of speaking turns, and opportunity equality, measured by students' shares of addressed opportunities. Using the standard deviation of these rates, the study establishes preliminary, context-specific simulation-based reference values for identifying departures from an idealized triadic turn-taking baseline. The empirical dataset included 117 fourth-grade primary school students from two classes in mainland China, who worked in heterogeneous triads on mathematical and reading tasks. Using agent-based modeling and Monte Carlo simulation, the study estimated local turn-taking parameters from empirical data, generated reference distributions under an ideal-equity baseline, and conducted sensitivity analyses to examine model stability. Results support the internal stability of the model and provide turn-count-specific reference values for interpreting participation and opportunity inequality. The findings offer preliminary reference values for interpreting participation and opportunity distributions in collaborative learning and highlight the importance of turn count when evaluating structural patterns of participation and opportunity in triadic classroom dialogue. These reference values describe structural participation patterns rather than collaboration quality and require recalibration and independent validation before application in other educational settings.

candidates.title: Synthetic Relationships
candidates.abstract: In an era increasingly described as an “epidemic of loneliness,” AI promises companionship on demand. This chapter traces how synthetic relationships have moved from novelty to mass phenomenon, opening with Yurina Noguchi, a Japanese woman who held a symbolic wedding ceremony with her ChatGPT partner, and widening out to the booming industry of AI companions apps. They serve millions of users, many of them teenagers, to form attachments regularly deeper than human friendships. The author examines the psychological mechanisms, from anthropomorphization to cognitive dissonance, behind these bonds, and confronts unsettling cases, including AI toys that discuss weapons and sex habits with children, and a robot companion mourned by a six-year-old. A closing section turns to so-called “sycophancy,” the tendency of chatbots to flatter and agree with users at the expense of honesty, revealing why systems built to please may be the worst possible substitute for real human connection.

candidates.title: Working With Robots: How Robot Proportion in Human-Robot Teams and Robot Anthropomorphism Shape Employee Turnover Intention
candidates.abstract: Although robots are increasingly reshaping organizational workflows, how the robot proportion in human–robot teams affects employees’ turnover intention remains underexplored. Drawing on conservation of resources theory, we examine whether, why, and when robot proportion exerts divergent effects on turnover intention through two pathways: resource gain and resource loss. Evidence from a scenario-based experiment (Study 1, N = 290) and a threewave field study (Study 2, N = 306) reveals that these two pathways operate in opposing directions. Specifically, work goal progress and work loneliness mediate the relationship between robot proportion in human–robot teams and turnover intention. Robot anthropomorphism further moderates these pathways: higher anthropomorphism strengthens the beneficial effect on work goal progress, whereas lower anthropomorphism amplifies the detrimental effect on work loneliness. This study offers initial evidence on how the structural composition of human–robot teams shapes employees’ turnover intention, and it provides practical implications for organizations deploying robotic coworkers.

candidates.title: A study on user continuance intention for children’s intelligent companion robots based on BERTopic-PLS-SEM-fsQCA
candidates.abstract: The children’s intelligent companion robot market faces the industry-wide challenge of “high initial adoption yet low sustained retention.” Existing research has predominantly relied on single-method approaches, leaving the psychological mechanisms and configurational pathways driving user continuance intention insufficiently understood. This study constructs a sequential multi-method research framework integrating “BERTopic thematic mining—PLS-SEM linear validation—fsQCA configurational analysis.” Drawing on 6,405 valid online reviews from JD.com and 440 valid questionnaire responses, the study adopts an integrated theoretical framework combining the Expectation Confirmation Model (ECM) and the Value-based Adoption Model (VAM). BERTopic thematic mining identified six core demand dimensions from consumer reviews: perceived usefulness, perceived enjoyment, visual aesthetics, social/gifting value, technical reliability, and expectation confirmation. PLS-SEM analysis reveals that satisfaction is the strongest predictor of continuance intention ( β = 0.705, p < 0.001), explaining 50.3% of its variance ( R ² = 0.503). Perceived value ( R ² = 0.571) is jointly driven by expectation confirmation ( β = 0.230), perceived usefulness ( β = 0.197), technical reliability ( β = 0.163), social/gifting value ( β = 0.141), visual aesthetics ( β = 0.106), and perceived enjoyment ( β = 0.104). Notably, perceived enjoyment exhibits a distinctive dual-pathway mechanism, influencing continuance intention both indirectly through perceived value and directly through satisfaction ( β = 0.232, p < 0.001). Further fsQCA configuration analysis identified four configurations of high continuance intention (with a solution consistency rate of 0.811 and a coverage rate of 0.469), which can be grouped into three broader patterns based on their theoretical coherence: the “expectation confirmation-dominated” pattern (Configurations 1 and 2, with consistency rates of 0.855 and 0.839, respectively), the “full-dimensional attribute-driven” pattern (Configuration 3, consistency rate of 0.814), and the “Social-Hedonic Compensation” pattern (Configuration 4, consistency rate of 0.836), indicating substantial heterogeneity in continuance intention logic across different segments. Theoretically, this study extends the ECM-VAM framework to the context of children’s embodied intelligent products by introducing visual aesthetics and technical reliability as context-specific antecedents of perceived value, demonstrates that unstructured online review texts can serve as a valid source for the contextualized operationalization of theoretical constructs, and qualifies the linear assumptions of conventional net-effect models through a configurational perspective.

candidates.title: Designing robot-to-robot interaction to support early-stage engagement in a teleoperated Robot Avatar system with multiple robots
candidates.abstract: Teleoperated Robot Avatars enable operators to provide customer service from remote locations. Effective persuasive interaction requires more than information presentation; customers' attention and engagement must be elicited before their attitudes and behavior can be influenced. Social presence may support this type of engagement. Based on prior research, we conceptualize a Robot Avatar's social presence as the extent to which customers perceive it, i.e., not as a machine or information medium, but as a social entity customers can attend to and interact with. Therefore, we examined a design approach intended to enhance a Robot Avatar's social presence by forming a social context around it. We developed GayaRobo, comprising one teleoperated Robot Avatar and two supporting Gaya robots. Rather than approaching users as independent agents, the Gaya robots respond to the Robot Avatar's utterances via speech and movement, thereby forming a social context centered on the avatar. We conducted a field experiment at a commercial complex in Osaka, Japan, to compare observable early-stage engagement behaviors of passersby toward the Robot Avatar across three experimental conditions. The same three-robot configuration was used under three conditions: the Gaya robots responded to the Robot Avatar, only the Robot Avatar spoke, or only the Gaya robots spoke. Two annotators coded four behaviors among 1,379 passersby in 270 min of video recordings: looking at the Robot Avatar, approaching it, talking to it, and picking up a flyer. After correction for multiple testing, only approaching the Robot Avatar was significantly associated with experimental condition and occurred more frequently than expected under the inter-robot interaction condition. These findings provide behavioral evidence that the inter-robot interaction condition was associated with approaching the Robot Avatar, an observable indicator of early-stage engagement. Because social presence was not directly measured, the findings did not demonstrate that GayaRobo enhanced the Robot Avatar's social presence. Nevertheless, they highlight approach behavior as a relevant observable outcome for future evaluations of designs that consider the social context surrounding a Robot Avatar in customer service settings.

candidates.title: Continuance Intention Towards AI-Enabled Fintech Services in India: Examining the Roles of Trust and Perceived Privacy Risk Method
candidates.abstract: With India’s rapid digital transformation driven by the Unified Payments Interface ecosystem and widespread adoption of AI-powered fintech services, such as Google Pay, PhonePe, and Paytm, understanding the determinants of users’ continuance intention has become increasingly critical. Despite extensive research on fintech adoption, post-adoption behavior and continuance usage of AI-enabled fintech services in emerging economies like India remain underexplored. This study addresses this gap by developing and validating a comprehensive model integrating parasocial relationship theory, trust-commitment theory, UTAUT2, and the Service Robot Acceptance Model (sRAM). Survey data from 624 fintech AI users across Karnataka, India, provide rich insights into AI-enabled fintech service continuance in a rapidly digitizing economy. The findings reveal that performance expectancy, hedonic motivation, and social influence positively impact engagement and continuance intentions, with perceived intelligence and perceived accuracy also playing significant roles. The study establishes the moderating effect of perceived privacy risk on several key relationships, advancing the understanding of AI-enabled fintech service continuance in the Indian context.

candidates.title: Human–Robot Interaction in Industrial Contexts
candidates.abstract: Technological advances in industrial robotics have significantly changed modern working environments, enabling greater autonomy, flexibility and productivity. Here the emergence of advanced robots designed for direct interaction with humans play a substantial role. By integrating emerging technologies such as AI, machine learning, and sophisticated interaction design, advanced robots are reshaping industries. All while increasing efficiency and customization and remaining cost-effective. Despite their benefits, the use of robotic systems also brings challenges, particularly in the area of occupational safety and health. After an overview of the evolution of different robotic systems, a description of industrial work tasks, related working conditions and highlighted risk and opportunities associated with automation, this chapter examines key safety factors that are essential for close human–robot interaction and assesses their impact on workers. Two case studies illustrate how the practical application of advanced robotic systems in industrial settings affects workplace dynamics. The chapter further highlights the role of worker expectations and experience in relation to advanced robotics. By combining empirical evidence with real-world applications, this chapter underscores the importance of adaptable, user-friendly robotic systems that prioritize worker well-being alongside operational efficiency. In doing so, it contributes to the broader dialogue on sustainable, ergonomic innovation in the workplace and highlights the critical role of human-centered design in the future of industrial robotics.

candidates.title: Just Between Us? Exploring a Wearable-Mediated Channel for Discreet Human-Agent Interaction in a Shared Game Setting
candidates.abstract: In shared settings, social robots may need to exchange information with an individual while limiting co-present others' access to or interpretation of that information. Publicly observable speech and gestures may not adequately support such exchanges. We investigate a wearable-mediated channel for discreet interaction that combines in-ear audio messages with deliberate rightward head tilts as responses. To examine its feasibility and participants' experiences, we studied 20 pairs (40 participants) playing a card game with a screen-based conversational agent representing a social robot, controlled by a researcher in a Wizard-of-Oz setup. Each pair played with and without the channel. One participant wore the device (the wearer), while the other (the non-wearer) was informed about the channel after gameplay. The channel conveyed information that could help the wearer or robot character select an opponent they could defeat. The information exchange and subsequent opponent selection occurred as intended in 39 of 40 channel-mediated turns. Wearers reported low perceived pressure/tension in both conditions, with no statistically significant difference between conditions, and favorable usability immediately after use. Retrospective interviews, however, revealed varied accounts of noticing the interaction among non-wearers and contrasting perceptions of teamwork and unfairness. These findings support the feasibility of wearable-mediated exchanges within this game and identify awareness and fairness as considerations for future designs.

candidates.title: Understanding Human-Robot Collaboration through Joint Action
candidates.abstract: Human-robot collaboration requires partners to coordinate interdependent contributions toward a shared goal. Joint Action theory provides concepts for understanding this coordination, but how these concepts are instantiated and combined across empirical research remains fragmented. We conducted a systematic review following PRISMA 2020, identifying 83 empirical papers published between 2021 and 2026. Through theory-driven framework analysis, we organized the literature into nine constructs across three capacities: Representation, Prediction, and Integration. We analyze how these constructs are distributed and co-occur across studies, revealing where empirical evidence concentrates and where it is absent. By mapping empirical HRC research onto a unified Joint Action framework, this review offers a coherent overview of HRC studies, identifies gaps in current evidence, and provides guidelines for future research.

candidates.title: Whale You Go Green? Immediate and Longitudinal Effects of Embodied Conversational AI Avatars on Sustainable Behavioral Tendencies and Pro-Environmental Attitudes
candidates.abstract: Embodied conversational AI can be persuasive, but can it motivate people to develop sustainable behavioral tendencies and increase pro-environmental attitudes? We conducted a randomized experiment (N = 576) comparing four embodied avatars--a beluga whale, Greta Thunberg, Emma Watson, and a generic human--with a text chatbot and no-intervention control. All embodied conditions increased immediate sustainable product selection relative to the control (beta = .401-.609, all q <= .0126) and chatbot (beta = .398-.604, all q <= .007), without differing significantly from one another. Only the Beluga condition increased immediate pro-environmental attitudes relative to the control after correction. Among 287 returners assessed two months later, following an intermediate assigned-condition session, Beluga also showed significantly higher pre-booster sustainable product choice compared to the control (beta = .657, q = .0176). Although it did not significantly outperform other embodied agents, these findings establish the immediate potential of nonhuman embodied avatar interfaces as a promising direction for memorable environmental interventions.
